name: Adam Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Adam. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead setter on the CNC lathes at Kessel Components. We turn brake discs and hub parts for two car makers. A CNC lathe is a machine that cuts metal following a program, and my job is setting it up, loading the right tools, running the first piece and measuring it before the run goes. I've got four lads on my shift and six machines, and I'm usually the one with a micrometer in my hand at the end of the line.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part and the hardest part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is when a new job runs perfect on the first piece. You feel like a craftsman for a second. Hardest part is the money, honestly. I'm one of the best setters in the building and I'm still paid less than the guys at the big plants on the motorway, and there are only two places like this within an hour of home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So nothing really moves. I can picture that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, a bit. Half the canteen was sure robots would take the lot by next year. I'd say the real fight is still pay and hours, same as it was before anyone said AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's safe in that world, Kessel's order book is full till 2028. But safe and comfortable aren't the same. Leila (my girlfriend) is in nursing school and I'm covering most of the rent, and I've got about three weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep setting the lathes and keep my overtime. I'd ask the union rep, Dave, to push for the setter grade that we've been promised for two years, which is about eighty more a month. And I'd keep using the AI thing on my phone for small stuff, like checking the wording on a union letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit stuck, like the treadmill keeps going and I keep running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said safe isn't comfortable. What would make it comfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two months saved instead of three weeks, and Leila finished with her course. She qualifies in eighteen months and then there are two wages. That's the finish line I'm running towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use the AI tool for now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I asked it once how to explain surface finish to a new starter, and it was decent. I don't use it for setting, because the lathe doesn't care what a chatbot thinks.

say: He'd tell the canteen **AI was overblown** and the fight is still about pay.
He'd point to the **setter grade** the union has chased for two years.
think: His job is safe with Kessel's **order book** full until 2028.
With **three weeks** saved and covering rent, safe still isn't comfortable.
do: Ask the union rep to push the **setter grade**, worth about eighty a month.
Use the **AI app** occasionally for writing small things.
feel: Mostly **fine**, but **stuck** on a treadmill of tight money.
S0.quote: Safe and comfortable aren't the same.
fieldNote: His job feels **secure**, but the household runs on his single wage.
He counts down to his partner's **nursing qualification** as the turning point.
He uses AI lightly and sees **no use** for it at the lathe itself.

steps.text: Ask union rep Dave to push the promised setter grade
Keep taking weekend overtime on the lathes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first, so the office and the planners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs to be in the room when Kessel buys new software, not told after. At the pub I'd say it's not the lathe that's in trouble, it's Sandra in purchasing, and that's wrong too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, it's probably not bad at first. The program for the lathe might get written by AI, and that's part of my job, but the setting up and measuring is hands. What worries me is fewer new starters, because if there are fewer of us, the shift gets harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be first to try any new programming software, because I'd rather learn it than be told by it. I'd go on the union's training committee. And I'd put my overtime money into savings instead of the car fund for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit edgy, but more curious than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask to try the software first. Is that you, or is that the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. I don't jump at new stuff, but once I see it work on someone else's machine, I'm in. And if I'm the one who knows the new programming software, I'm harder to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jamal, my youngest on the shift. He's nineteen, and right now he's learning programming from me. If the AI writes the programs, he never learns, and he's the first one gone.

say: The union must be **in the room** when Kessel buys new software.
The **purchasing staff** are most at risk, and that's wrong too.
think: Hands-on **setting and measuring** keep his job safe at first.
**Fewer new starters** would make every shift harder.
do: Volunteer to **trial** any new programming software.
Put **overtime money** into savings instead of the car fund.
S1.quote: If I'm the one who knows the new programming software, I'm harder to cut.
fieldNote: He frames learning as **protection**, waiting to see it work before committing.
His sharpest worry is for **young trainees** like Jamal who may never learn the trade.
He backs **union involvement** in tech decisions, not resistance to the tech.

steps.text: Volunteer to trial Kessel's new lathe programming software
Move overtime pay into savings for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking, five for the hands. Wow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a law, not a pep talk. If companies can replace everyone, then they should pay for what comes next. I'd march for that, and I'm not really the marching type.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think the programming side of my job is gone by 2028, so I become a man who loads parts and measures them. Then by 2031 a robot loads and measures too. That's me at thirty-two with nothing, and Leila just qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Leila about whether I should go into nursing or care too, because people might still want a person there. I'd stop the car fund completely and put every spare penny away. And I'd join whatever union campaign there was for a wage guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cold. Like the floor's gone out from under the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nursing might still need people. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some days. Leila says the robots can lift but they can't hold someone's hand when they're dying. I hope she's right, but I'm not betting the rent on hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get to watch it happen in slow motion. The office goes, then the programming, then me. Three years isn't enough to retrain on what I earn with what I've saved.

say: This needs **a law**, with companies paying for what comes next.
He'd join a **march** despite not being the marching type.
think: The **programming** side of his job goes by 2028, leaving loading and measuring.
By **2031** robots take the rest, leaving him at thirty-two with nothing.
do: Discuss switching into **nursing or care** with Leila.
Stop the **car fund** and save every spare penny.
Join a union campaign for a **wage guarantee**.
feel: **Cold**, as if the floor has gone from under his plans.
S2.quote: Three years isn't enough to retrain on what I earn with what I've saved.
fieldNote: He maps his job **task by task** against the two dates precisely.
Partner's **care work** looks to him like a possible refuge, but he doubts it.
The short warning pushes this cautious man toward **protest**.

steps.text: Talk with Leila about training for care or nursing work
Close the car fund and save all spare money
March with the union for a wage guarantee law

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a real runway, but short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get the training in now, while there's time, and make the companies pay for it. At work I'd push the union to bargain for paid retraining in the next contract, not the one after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is my sweet spot to move, if I see others move first. By 2031 the programming's gone, so I'd want to be on the maintenance side by then, fixing the robots that come in 2034. That's the job that lasts longest, I reckon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a mechatronics course, that's mechanics and electronics together, at the technical college, one night a week. I'd use the AI tool more to study, since it's patient at two in the morning. And I'd keep my overtime for the fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Determined, with a knot in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you move once others move. Who would you be watching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate Kofi left our plant for a robot maintenance job at the warehouse last year. If Kofi's still in work in two years, that's my proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut to pay for college?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car fund again, and the takeaway on Fridays. Leila's going to love that.

say: Get **training in now** and make companies pay for it.
Push the union for **paid retraining** in the next contract.
think: Five years is his **sweet spot** to move, once others go first.
**Robot maintenance** looks like the job that lasts longest.
do: Enrol in a **mechatronics** course one night a week.
Use the **AI tool** to help study at night.
S3.quote: My mate Kofi left our plant for a robot maintenance job at the warehouse last year. If Kofi's still in work in two years, that's my proof.
fieldNote: He needs **proof from peers** like Kofi before committing.
Five years gives him a concrete **retraining path** into maintenance.
Money stays the **limit**: fees come from overtime and Friday takeaways.

steps.text: Enrol in a one-night-a-week mechatronics course at the college
Study course material with the AI app at night
Drop Friday takeaways and the car fund to pay fees
Push the union to bargain for paid retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it properly, with apprenticeships for robot work and a plan for every plant. I'd say it in union meetings and I'd vote for whoever had that plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd relax a bit too much in the first couple of years. I'd tell myself Leila's qualified, there are two wages, I can finally breathe. Then around year four I'd start the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd save properly now that there are two incomes, maybe a hundred a month. I'd keep setting at Kessel. I'd ask the union to set up a retraining scheme with the college so it's ready when I'm ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. Worried about later, not now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd relax too much. Is that a problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. But I've been running since I was eighteen. Two years of breathing wouldn't kill me, as long as I start before the thinking AI arrives in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Leila change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk about kids sooner rather than later, actually. If the big change comes at forty, I'd rather the kids were a bit older and we'd had some good years first.

say: A decade is time for **robot apprenticeships** and a plan for every plant.
He'd **vote** for whoever had that plan.
think: He'd **relax too much** in the first years, with two wages coming in.
He'd start retraining around **year four**, before thinking AI lands.
do: Save about **a hundred** a month once there are two incomes.
Ask the union to build a **retraining scheme** with the college.
feel: **Steady**, worried about later rather than now.
S4.quote: I've been running since I was eighteen. Two years of breathing wouldn't kill me
fieldNote: The long warning lets him **rest first**, which he admits might be a mistake.
He thinks about **having children** earlier to get good years in before the change.
His plans hinge on Leila's **second income** arriving.

steps.text: Save a hundred a month once Leila is working
Keep setting the CNC lathes at Kessel
Ask the union to set up a college retraining scheme
Talk with Leila about having children sooner

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Leila would only just be qualified and I'd be watching my job go in pieces. What would help is a proper law that makes the companies fund retraining, and a wage while you train, because I can't study and pay rent on nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the towns. Kessel is the reason half my street has a job. If the plant goes, the bakery goes, the pub goes, my mum's hairdresser goes.

headlineQuote: If the plant goes, the bakery goes, the pub goes, my mum's hairdresser goes.
portrait: Adam is a **27-year-old** lead CNC lathe setter at Kessel Components, a brake-parts plant.
He covers most of the rent while his girlfriend Leila **trains as a nurse**, with three weeks saved.
A **steady** progressive, he backs the union and waits for proof from peers before changing.
He uses AI **now and then**, mainly for writing, and sees **maintenance** as the lasting job.
The two-year warning alarms him; with **five or ten** years he plans mechatronics study.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, watching his job go in pieces just as Leila qualifies.
whatWouldHelp: A **law** making companies fund retraining, with a **wage while training**.
